title: Mesh adaptive direct search algorithms for constrained optimization
contribution: Introduces the MADS class, which decouples the mesh size from the poll size so that poll directions can become asymptotically dense; proves a hierarchy of Clarke-type (and contingent/KKT) stationarity results for extreme-barrier constrained nonsmooth problems under a nonempty-hypertangent CQ; and gives the randomized LTMADS instance with probability-one density and a four-problem comparison against GPS.
problem_entry: Own previous method's limitation: GPS polls finitely many directions, so its hierarchy gives f°(x̂;d)≥0 only on a finite set (Example F of the 2004 tightness paper), and with bound constraints no smoothness, penalty or filter fixes this; the goal is stated as inequality (1.4) (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Split GPS's single Δ into mesh size Δm and poll size Δp with Δm≤Δp and Δm→0 iff Δp→0, so frames on ever finer lattices can use ever more directions; keep mesh, simple decrease and free SEARCH from GPS; apply to f_Ω with constraints tested before f (pp. 4-5).
assumptions: x0∈Ω, f(x0) finite, iterates in a compact set; f Lipschitz (or strictly differentiable) near x̂; nonempty hypertangent cone (equivalent to a Gould-Tolle-type condition for C1 constraints, Thm 3.4); refining directions dense in T^H, which LTMADS delivers with probability 1 and only when the iterates converge to a single x̂ (pp. 1, 7-8, 12-13, 19).
proof_devices: minimal-frame inequality f(x_k+Δm d_k)≥f(x_k) read as one difference quotient of Jahn's constrained Clarke derivative with y=x_k, t=Δm‖d_k‖ (Thm 3.12, p. 12)
Jahn's Ω-restricted Clarke derivative so results depend on f, not the discontinuous f_Ω; not evaluating f outside Ω is needed by the proof (pp. 2, 4, 12)
Lipschitz continuity of f° across hypertangent directions and continuity onto the Clarke cone (Lemma 3.8, Prop 3.9, pp. 9-11), with Example 3.10 showing failure when T^H is empty (pp. 11-12)
Torczon lattice argument x_N = x0 + Σ Δm_k D z_k for liminf Δ = 0 (Prop 3.1, p. 7)
probability lower bound (ε/4)^(n-1)/(2n), independent of k, by counting integers for the reused direction b(ℓ) (Thm 4.3, p. 18)
integrality/determinant bookkeeping |det B|=2^(ℓn) to verify frame conditions (Prop 4.2, pp. 16-17)
hypertangent ⇔ ∇c_i^T v<0 on active constraints via the mean value theorem (Thm 3.4, p. 8)
experiments: 4 purpose-labelled problems vs GPS (NOMAD) with empty/simple SEARCH to isolate the POLL, objective vs #evaluations, 5 LTMADS runs: a 2-D GPS-stagnation function, catalytic-combustion fitting where GPS is known good (500-eval budget; MADS dynamic n+1 best), a hypersphere LP for four values of n (600n budget), and a hypothesis-violating narrowing region run to Δm<1e-323; no profiles, no other-family solver (pp. 4, 19-25).
positioning: Between GPS and Coope-Price frame methods, deliberately less general than Coope-Price for implementability; sharpest criticism aimed at the authors' own GPS hierarchy, tightness examples and filter GPS; Lewis-Torczon barrier reframed by what it needs to know (pp. 1-4, 26).
writing: Abstract states the main result and its two limits; first-person motivation ('in our opinion'); roadmap previews each example's point; pauses for intuition at the hypertangent definition; Newton/SQP analogy for hypotheses; discussion invites other instances (pp. 1, 3, 8, 13, 26).
limits_future: Probability-one only and needs whole-sequence convergence; feasible x0 required (filter planned); four examples not conclusive; stalls on narrowing feasible regions; GPS+random SEARCH similar at small n; deterministic instance and implicit-filtering templates left open (pp. 7, 19, 25-26).

title: Finding optimal algorithmic parameters using derivative-free optimization
contribution: Proposes a general framework that treats an algorithm's performance over an instance set as a blackbox function of its parameters, minimized by MADS with a surrogate built from easier instances, and uses it to find trust-region update constants that cut total CPU time on 55 large CUTEr problems by about 25% relative to the classical values (preprint read: 'Finding optimal algorithmic parameters using a mesh adaptive direct search', Dec 2004).
problem_entry: Folklore defaults: the classical trust-region constants (1/4, 3/4, 1/2, 2) recommended in six references are claimed 'arbitrary'; prior discretized sensitivity study cannot compare many variants since performance profiles are unclear beyond five or six, so comparison is delegated to an optimizer (pp. 2-3, 18).
key_idea: ψ(p) = aggregate performance (CPU time or evaluations) of algorithm A on a representative hard set; σ(p) = same measure on an easy set; MADS uses σ to warm start, to order POLL/SEARCH candidates and to prune SEARCH candidates only (threshold v=0.1), with LHS and random screened SEARCH (pp. 5-9, 15-16, 20).
assumptions: Compact iterates and finite start (Assumption 1); polyhedral/bound Ω with η1<η2 hard-coded as barrier; α2≤10 added partly to satisfy Assumption 1; scaling (1000,100,100,10); admitted that optimality is ill-defined and ψ is not a function because CPU time is noisy (pp. 3-4, 8, 16-18).
proof_devices: no new proofs: MADS hierarchy specialized to bounds with an added lower-semicontinuity rung (Thm 2.5, p. 10) and used as a design rule (POLL candidates may be ordered but never pruned, pp. 6, 10)
barrier encoding of a linear parameter constraint so the theory sees only bounds (p. 18)
failure → +∞ convention for iteration limits, memory errors and floating-point exceptions (pp. 17-18)
experiments: 163 CUTEr unconstrained problems → surrogate list (54 problems, n<1000, 68 s) and objective list (55 problems, n≥1000, 13461 s per evaluation) by explicit rules; phase 1 on σ2 (310 evals, truth 13461→11498 s, ≈1% re-evaluation noise), phase 2 on ψ2 with 150 truth evals ≈3 weeks (→10192 s, −25%); performance profiles in CPU time and evaluations on the same list used for tuning; outlier analysis (GENHUMPS, CRAGGLVY) (pp. 19-25).
positioning: Reframes the discretized sensitivity study of Gould-Orban-Sartenaer-Toint (a co-author's) by its scaling problem; addresses smooth-optimization readers with a trust-region review and DFO readers with a MADS review; blackbox motivation drawn from the authors' network (helicopter rotor, maintenance) (pp. 3-4, 11, 18).
writing: 'Twofold' abstract; one strong claim ('Our contention...') then hedged discussion; counterintuitive result attributed to the measure, not the optimizer; noise caveat in a footnote; humor in the literature review (pp. 1, 11, 16, 18, 23-24).
limits_future: Result depends on the chosen measure; global sums ignore slow failures and variability; noise; continuous bounded parameters only; future: outlier-aware objectives, MADS scaling strategies, integer/categorical/constrained parameters (pp. 21, 23, 25-26).

title: Convergence of mesh adaptive direct search to second-order stationary points
contribution: Extends Abramson's second-order GPS analysis to MADS: derives set-constrained second-order necessary and sufficient conditions in terms of feasible directions, proves that with dense refining directions a C^{1,1} limit point satisfies the necessary condition and (under twice strict differentiability, local convexity and a nonsingular Hessian) is a strict local minimizer, and shows by an explicit GPS instance that GPS can converge to a saddle point that MADS excludes (preprint read: 'Second-Order Convergence of Mesh-Adaptive Direct Search', Aug 2005).
problem_entry: Extension of a special-case result (GPS second order) to the general class, hooked on a failure mode: GPS cannot converge to a local maximizer in infinitely many steps but can converge to a saddle; barrier gives no constraint gradients, so Lagrangian conditions are unavailable (pp. 1-2, 9).
key_idea: Dense refining directions plus C^{1,1} smoothness and the Hiriart-Urruty-Strodiot-Nguyen generalized Hessian yield second-order conditions along all feasible directions; no algorithmic change, GPS recovered as Δp=Δm (pp. 4, 8-13).
assumptions: Feasible finite x0, compact iterates; f C^{1,1} near x̂, T^H≠∅, Ω regular near x̂ (Thm 4.8); f twice strictly differentiable, Ω convex near x̂, ∇²f nonsingular (Thm 4.9); f's smoothness assumed independent of Ω so Taylor applies in any direction; density only almost sure in practice (pp. 5, 9, 12-13, 15-16).
proof_devices: central second difference: add Taylor expansions at x_k±t d_k, merge Hessian elements by convexity of ∂²f, + side ≥0 by minimal frame forces − side ≤γ<0, contradiction with ∇f^T v=0; mirror point never evaluated (Thm 4.8, pp. 12-13)
set-constrained second-order conditions via the cone of feasible directions, each bounded by an example (Thm 4.4 + Ex 4.5; Thm 4.6 + Ex 4.7; pp. 9-11)
local boundedness and closedness of the generalized Hessian mapping to pass to limits (pp. 8-11)
adversarial GPS instance (τ=2, w-=-4, w+=3, iteration-dependent poll order) proved by induction over a period-3 table to converge to a saddle (Ex 4.10, Prop 4.11, pp. 13-15)
experiments: none (illustrative examples and one figure of GPS iterates only, p. 14)
positioning: Builds on Abramson (GPS second order) and Hiriart-Urruty et al.; contrasts barrier with penalty and filter approaches; claims stronger results than GPS backed by two GPS failure examples; cites S016 as a SEARCH example (pp. 2-3, 8-9, 13).
writing: 'important and surprisingly strong' next to an 'unfortunately' negative; 'main contributions' label; each optimality theorem followed by a limiting example; pre-empts the '2n directions' misreading; conclusion admits density is not implementable (pp. 2, 10-13, 15-16).
limits_future: Density not implementable, results almost sure through LTMADS; regularity/local convexity required; future: clever deterministic enumeration of directions (the OrthoMADS problem); reader's check: Thm 4.9 as printed fails at boundary points (f=ab on R²₊ from 0), not stated in the paper (pp. 13, 15-16).

quotes.text: We show here that it may, unfortunately, converge in an infinite number of steps to a saddle point.
In practice, this is not possible because, as the algorithm converges, it would require increasingly more poll directions; in fact, an infinite number in the limit.
